analysis.one_liner: Rescinds remaining IRS funding for tax enforcement and a free direct e-filing system.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced Jan. 3, 2025 with 36 Republican cosponsors, has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee with no markup, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill cancels (rescinds) unspent money Congress gave the IRS in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act — money for tax enforcement and collections, for operations support including taxpayer services, and for a task force studying a free, government-run way to file taxes electronically [S2][S3]. It also cancels unspent funds for Treasury offices that oversee and support the IRS, including the Tax Court and the tax administration's inspector general [S2]. In plain terms, it shrinks the government's ability to collect taxes that are already owed, and kills the seed money for a free direct e-filing option.
analysis.who_benefits: If it became law, the largest gainers would be filers who underreport income or underpay taxes — disproportionately high earners, partnerships, and large companies — because a smaller enforcement staff catches less of it. The paid tax-preparation industry would also benefit, since the bill cancels funding for the task force studying a free, direct government e-filing system that would compete with paid software [S2]. Sponsors frame the benefit as protecting families and small businesses from IRS enforcement actions [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High-income underreporters and paid tax preparers

how_it_helps.text: Cancels unobligated IRS enforcement and collections money appropriated by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, reducing audit and collection capacity [S2][S3].
Cancels funds for the task force researching a free, direct electronic tax-filing system, ending that government alternative to paid filing software [S2].

Cancels unspent funds for Treasury oversight offices including the Tax Court and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, reducing scrutiny capacity as well as enforcement capacity [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Compliant taxpayers and the federal budget. Less enforcement means less revenue collected from people and companies that underpay, so either the deficit grows or other taxpayers effectively cover the gap. Ordinary filers also lose the potential free direct e-filing option the bill cancels funding for [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Compliant taxpayers and the federal treasury

drawbacks.text: The rescinded funds were specifically for tax determination and collection and for operations support, so enacting the bill means the IRS has less capacity to collect taxes already owed under current law [S2][S3].
Rescinding enforcement appropriations also cuts the taxpayer-services side of operations support, since the same funds covered both [S2].
Killing the free direct e-filing task force removes the only funded path toward a government-run free filing alternative to commercial software [S2].

A fair objection from supporters is that the 2022 appropriation was large and long-dated, and that some taxpayers want a smaller IRS with fewer enforcement contacts; the counterargument is that enforcement revenue generally exceeds its cost, so the rescission trades spending cuts for lost collections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real spending cut and, as its sponsors intend, less IRS enforcement activity directed at families and small businesses. The cost falls on tax collection itself: less money recovered from underpayment, which shifts the burden onto filers who pay what they owe, and the end of funded work on a free direct e-filing system. Weighing it, the gains are concentrated among those who underpay; the costs are spread across everyone else's tax bill and the deficit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on Jan. 3, 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Adrian Smith (R-NE) introduced the bill on Jan. 3, 2025, the first day of the 119th Congress, with 36 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is the standard first step for a tax bill [S5].
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote has been scheduled in the more than a year since referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, the status quo holds: IRS enforcement and collections funding from 2022 remains available, and high-income underreporters keep paying at existing enforcement levels rather than gaining a lower-risk environment. Paid tax-preparation firms likewise still face a funded federal study of a free direct-filing alternative rather than its cancellation [S2][S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one — the bill has gone nowhere

for.name: Rep. Adrian Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to rescind unobligated IRS funding on Jan. 3, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All listed cosponsors are Republicans — 36 of 223 House R members — with no Democratic cosponsors on record [S4]; the bill has not reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Paid tax preparation and filing software industry
industries.note: The bill cancels funding for the task force researching a free, direct government e-filing system, removing a future free competitor to paid filing software [S2]. Ordinary filers would keep paying commercial preparers and software fees.

industries.industry: High-income filers and large businesses with underreported taxes
industries.note: Rescinding IRS enforcement and collections funding means fewer resources aimed at finding and collecting taxes that are owed, which lowers the risk and cost of underpayment for those best positioned to do it [S2][S3]. The cost shows up as lost revenue that other taxpayers and the deficit absorb.

industries.industry: IRS and Treasury oversight offices (including the Tax Court and the tax administration inspector general)
industries.note: The bill rescinds unspent funds for these offices' operations, shrinking their capacity to administer the tax system and conduct oversight [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority and 36 cosponsors, the bill could in principle move through Ways and Means, but standalone IRS rescission bills at this stage typically stall in committee and are more likely to resurface folded into a larger tax or spending package than to receive their own floor vote. With no committee action in over a year, the default expectation is that it dies at the end of this Congress like similar prior-session bills.
